subtype: Approach: waiting to be noticed for hard work [Pitfall]
passage: Sushma had worked past nine on most nights for two years. She assumed the committee would notice, and so she never mentioned that she wanted a bigger role. Her manager thought of her as dependable, the one who fixed things quietly. When the promotion committee met, with only one slot in the year's budget, her manager described her as reliable and could not say what bigger role she was ready for. Arnab, who had asked in March what the next level needed and led one small project, was promoted. Sushma heard it at the tea counter and smiled, then went back to her desk and stared at the screen without typing.

qa.q: How late did Sushma work on most nights?
qa.a: Sushma worked past nine on most nights.

qa.q: How was Sushma feeling at the tea counter?
qa.a: Sushma was hurt and deflated, though she smiled, and afterwards she stared at the screen without typing.

qa.q: What could Sushma do next, and why?
qa.a: Sushma could tell her manager she wants a bigger role and ask what it takes, because the committee can only weigh a case that someone has made.

qa.q: How might Sushma's manager have seen her at the committee?
qa.a: The manager saw a reliable person but had no goal or bigger-role evidence to present, so there was nothing to argue for.

grounding: Illustrates assuming long hours will speak for themselves and never discussing a goal, so the committee sees reliability but no case and a colleague who asked is promoted.

subtype: Approach: waiting to be noticed for hard work [Pitfall]
passage:
Afreen was usually the last person at the Bandra office, switching off the AC in the empty design floor at nine.
She had decided long ago that hard work would say everything for her. She never mentioned the word "promotion" to her manager. Talking about herself felt like bragging.
Vikas, who sat opposite, was different. In March he booked a meeting with their manager and asked plainly what the senior role needed. He came out with a list and pinned it above his monitor.
In July the promotions were announced. Vikas's name was there. Afreen's wasn't.
Later her manager told her kindly, "The committee sees you as very reliable. But nobody presented a case for you leading. I didn't know you wanted it."
Afreen sat at her desk long after everyone left, staring at the dark screen, all those late nights suddenly feeling like a private hobby.

qa.q: What was Afreen feeling as she stared at the dark screen?
qa.a: Afreen felt hurt and deflated, realising her late nights had gone unseen because she never said what she wanted.

qa.q: What else could Afreen have done in March, like Vikas?
qa.a: She could have asked the manager directly what the senior role needed and by when, turning her effort into a case the committee could see.

qa.q: How does the outcome look to Vikas?
qa.a: Vikas got the role by asking and following a clear list, and he may feel pleased but a little awkward, knowing Afreen worked just as hard.

grounding: It shows someone assuming long hours will speak for themselves, never discussing the goal, and watching a colleague who asked get promoted.

subtype: Approach: waiting to be noticed for hard work [Pitfall]
passage:
"Congratulations, Jomon. Team lead. Wow." Sarika held out her hand across the canteen table.
"Thanks. Honestly, I thought you'd get it."
"So did I." She laughed, but it came out thin. "I've been here earlier than anyone for two years. I stayed every time a release slipped."
"I know. Everyone knows."
"Then how did you get it?"
Jomon stirred his tea. "I asked Mr. Paul last year what the role needed. He said client handling and planning. So I volunteered for both and told him every time I did."
"I never asked him anything. I thought if I worked hard enough, he'd notice."
"He noticed you work hard. At the panel he said you're the most dependable person here."
"Dependable." Sarika looked at her samosa. "That's what you say about a bus."
Jomon didn't know what to say to that.

qa.q: What did Mr. Paul say the team lead role needed?
qa.a: He said client handling and planning.

qa.q: What was Sarika feeling when her laugh came out thin?
qa.a: She was disappointed and hurt, trying to seem happy for Jomon while realising her hard work alone hadn't earned the role.

qa.q: What would you change first in Sarika's approach before the next round?
qa.a: She could ask Mr. Paul directly what a lead role needs and agree how to show it, instead of waiting for her effort to be noticed.

qa.q: What is it like for Jomon during this conversation?
qa.a: Jomon feels awkward and a little guilty, glad to be promoted but unsure how to comfort a colleague he expected would get it.

grounding: It shows someone who assumed hard work would be noticed and never discussed the goal, while a colleague who asked was promoted.
